Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2023 May 1. Published in final edited form as: J Clin Child Adolesc Psychol. 2021 Sep 27;51(3):295–311. doi: 10.1080/15374416.2021.1969654 Abstract Objective: Interpersonal negative life events (NLEs) have been linked to risk for suicidal thoughts and behaviors. However, little is known about how this risk is conferred over the short term and the mechanisms linking interpersonal NLEs to suicide risk, particularly in adolescents. This study used an intensive longitudinal design to examine thwarted belongingness with family and friends as potential mechanisms linking interpersonal NLEs to suicidal thoughts. Method: Forty-eight adolescents (Mage = 14.96 years; 64.6% female, 77.1% White), who recently received acute psychiatric care for suicide risk, were followed intensely for 28 days after discharge. Smartphone-based ecological momentary assessment was used to measure presence of interpersonal NLEs at the day level, fluctuations in thwarted belongingness with family and friends (separately) within day, and fluctuations in suicidal thoughts within day. A multi-level structural equation model was utilized to examine family thwarted belongingness and friend thwarted belongingness as parallel mediators in the relationship between interpersonal NLEs and next-day suicidal thoughts. Results: Significant direct effects were observed between interpersonal NLEs and family thwarted belongingness, family thwarted belongingness and suicidal thoughts, and friend thwarted belongingness and suicidal thoughts. In addition, family, but not friend, thwarted belongingness significantly mediated the association between interpersonal NLEs and next-day suicidal thoughts. Conclusions: Interpersonal NLEs predicted greater suicidal thoughts over the short term (next day) in high-risk adolescents. Findings suggest how interpersonal NLEs may confer risk for suicidal thoughts—by reducing feelings of family belongingness. Future research is needed to examine how modifying belongingness may reduce suicide risk in adolescents. STBs are related to significant academic and social impairment (Copeland et al., 2017; Foley et al., 2006) and confer risk for suicide death (Ribeiro et al., 2016). Suicidal thoughts typically begin during the transition to adolescence and rates increase significantly during this developmental period (Nock et al., 2008; Nock et al., 2013). Moreover, for about a third of adolescents, escalation from suicidal thoughts to suicide attempts (i.e., deliberate, self-inflicted injury with at least some intent to die; Silverman et al., 2007) will occur within one to two years after the onset of suicidal thoughts (Glenn et al., 2017; Nock et al., 2008; Nock et al., 2013). Recent estimates from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s 2019 Youth Risk Behavior Survey suggest that approximately 19% of high school students thought about suicide in the past year and 9% attempted suicide at least once (Ivey-Stephenson et al., 2020). Alarmingly, STB-related hospitalizations have doubled for youth over the past decade (Plemmons et al., 2018). Effective suicide prevention for youth will require a range of upstream (i.e., build protective factors) and downstream (i.e., crisis intervention) approaches (JED Foundation, 2017; Suicide Prevention Resource Center, 2020). To enhance downstream suicide prevention approaches, the field needs knowledge about when youth are most at risk and what factors may be modifiable during this time to reduce risk. Although considerable research has aimed to identify potential suicide risk factors (Franklin et al., 2017), this work has been limited in its examination of short-term risk factors and high-risk periods (Glenn & Nock, 2014). For instance, one of the highest risk periods for suicidal behavior and suicide-related rehospitalizations is the month following discharge from psychiatric hospitalization (Chung et al., 2017). This also is a time period with significant fluctuations in suicide ideation among adolescents (Prinstein et al., 2008). However, far less is known about how risk is conferred during the post-hospitalization period. One factor that has been related to suicide risk, and may help to clarify risk processes during this time, is the presence of negative life events (NLEs), specifically interpersonal NLEs. Interpersonal negative life events and suicide risk NLEs have been linked to risk for STBs across the lifespan (Liu & Miller, 2014). The range of NLEs that have been associated with STBs can be broadly categorized as either interpersonal (e.g., loss, difficulties or conflict with family, friends, and romantic partners) or non-interpersonal events (e.g., health, financial, legal). This distinction between interpersonal and non-interpersonal NLEs is important given research indicating that interpersonal NLEs are robustly related to suicide risk (Bagge et al., 2013; Brent et al., 1993; Liu & Miller, 2014; Stewart et al., 2019). Among adolescents, interpersonal NLEs related to family (e.g., conflict, rejection), peers (e.g., rejection, exclusion, victimization), and romantic partners (e.g., relationship break-ups) are the most strongly linked to STBs (Beautrais et al., 1997; Cheek, Goldston, et al., 2020; Fergusson et al., 2000; Holt et al., 2015). fetched_contents.text: The Use of Intensive Longitudinal Methods in Research on Suicidal Thoughts and Behaviors: A Systematic Review Arch Suicide Res. 2022 Jul-Sep;26(3):1007-1021. doi: 10.1080/13811118.2021.1903635. Epub 2021 Apr 1. * PMID: 33794112 * DOI: 10.1080/13811118.2021.1903635 Abstract Objective: Intensive longitudinal methods (ILM), such as ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and daily diary, involve repeatedly assessing individuals over short periods of time and have been increasingly used to study suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs). Suicidal thoughts have been shown to vary over short periods of time and reports of STBs are subject to negative biases. Therefore, ILM are important methodological tools for studying STBs, ones that capture enhanced precision and realism of data compared to traditional survey methods. The present systematic review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of ILM used to study STBs, including the various EMA and daily diary methodologies used, the feasibility of those methodologies, and the ethical considerations in this line of research. This review also summarizes the characteristics of descriptive STB outcomes specific to the ILM data collection period. Methods: A thorough search of PubMed and PsycINFO was conducted up to May 2020, resulting in twenty-eight papers reviewed. Results and conclusions: The review of the studies showed that ILM are largely feasible and do not have a negative impact on participants. In addition, the reviewed studies revealed unique aspects of STBs, such as the variability of suicidal thoughts, that suggest that ILM are important methodologies to use when studying STBs. Gaps in the research and recommendations for future research are discussed.HighlightsIt is feasible to use ILM to study suicidality.ILM do not have a negative impact on participants with suicidality.Few studies have used ILM to study suicidality in diverse samples. Authors Affiliations * 1 Department of Psychology, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA. * 2 National Center for Veterans Studies, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA. * PMID: 33624868 * DOI: 10.1111/sltb.12662 Abstract Interpersonal risk and resilience factors are prominent in current conceptual models of suicide. A growing body of empirical evidence links suicidal thoughts and behaviors to a range of interpersonal phenomenon adding further support to the value of this line of inquiry. At present, research on interpersonal phenomenon focuses on assessing individuals' perceptions of interpersonal phenomenon, such as appraisals of burdensomeness, experienced loneliness, and thwarted belongingness. As this line of research continues to develop, we argue that it would be valuable to consider incorporating conceptual models of interpersonal phenomenon and corresponding methodological approaches from closely allied fields. After providing a brief overview of interpersonal models of suicide, we present an introduction to conceptual models of interpersonal phenomenon developed in relationship science, describe how these models can be applied to the study of interpersonal phenomenon in suicide research, and close with a guided tutorial on data collection and statistical analysis methods for testing hypotheses derived from these conceptual approaches. References for additional reading are provided, and the Appendix S1 provides simulated data sets and statistical code for the analyses in the tutorial section. Abstract Longitudinal models are becoming increasingly prevalent in the behavioral sciences, with key advantages including increased power, more comprehensive measurement, and establishment of temporal precedence. One particularly salient strength offered by longitudinal data is the ability to disaggregate between-person and within-person effects in the regression of an outcome on a time-varying covariate. However, the ability to disaggregate these effects has not been fully capitalized upon in many social science research applications. Two likely reasons for this omission are the general lack of discussion of disaggregating effects in the substantive literature and the need to overcome several remaining analytic challenges that limit existing quantitative methods used to isolate these effects in practice. This review explores both substantive and quantitative issues related to the disaggregation of effects over time, with a particular emphasis placed on the multilevel model. Existing analytic methods are reviewed, a general approach to the problem is proposed, and both the existing and proposed methods are demonstrated using several artificial data sets. Potential limitations and directions for future research are discussed, and recommendations for the disaggregation of effects in practice are offered. Keywords: multilevel modeling, growth modeling, trajectory analysis, within-person effects INTRODUCTION Many central theories in psychology and allied fields either implicitly or explicitly focus on within-person processes. For example, when an individual engages in effective coping, this is thought to mitigate the effects of stress for this individual (e.g., Roth & Cohen 1986). Similarly, when a person experiences negative affect, this person is expected to be more likely to engage in alcohol or substance use (e.g., Kassel et al. 2010). Finally, when an individual exercises more, it is expected that his or her positive affect will subsequently increase (e.g., Penedo & Dahn 2005). These three examples all highlight that the underlying theory posits what will happen within a given individual (that is, with respect to intraindividual processes), but not across a set of individuals (that is, with respect to interindividual processes). Despite the fact that the majority of psychological theories posit within-person processes, the research conducted to empirically evaluate these theories often involves the collection and analysis of strictly between-person data. Such between-person data almost always take the form of cross-sectional (or single time point) assessments of behavior. However, as has long been known, such data are poorly suited for evaluating within-person processes (Molenaar 2004, Schaie 1965). For example, if at a single point in time one person reports being both depressed and alcohol dependent and another person reports being neither depressed nor alcohol dependent, this does not imply that either person will drink more alcohol when experiencing negative affect. Thus, theory explicitly posits an effect at one level of analysis, yet standard cross-sectional designs and associated statistical models test an effect at a different level of analysis (e.g., Curran & Willoughby 2003). Fortunately, there is growing recognition in our field that greater emphasis must be placed on the study of within-person processes and that this can only be accomplished through the study of intraindividual differences in repeated measures data (Collins 2006; Molenaar 2004; Molenaar & Newell 2010; Nesselroade 1991a,b; Raudenbush 2001a,b). Long- and short-term longitudinal studies are therefore becoming increasingly prevalent, including both traditional designs (e.g., Goldstein 1981) as well as newer experience sampling and ecological momentary assessment approaches (e.g., Walls & Schafer 2006). Despite this encouraging trend, the importance of focusing on within-person processes is still not universally appreciated. Interestingly, it is common to see the articulated strengths of longitudinal data designs to include factors such as the establishment of temporal precedence, the reduction of alternative potential models, and increases in statistical power (e.g., Muthén & Curran 1997). However, it is much less common to see an emphasis placed on the fact that only longitudinal data allow for the proper separation of between-person and within-person effects and that this is critically needed for fully evaluating many theories in psychology. We are thus faced with a curious juxtaposition of recent developments. On the one hand, it is comforting to see that a clear emphasis has been placed on the importance of collecting and analyzing longitudinal data; yet on the other hand, it does not appear that a similar emphasis has been placed on the testing of within- and between-person influences on behavior once such data are obtained. The net result is that, although empirical data are increasingly available that will allow for the direct disaggregation of within-person and between person effects, this important opportunity is not often fully capitalized upon, if capitalized upon at all. There is certainly a variety of reasons why many researchers do not take full advantage of the data that are available to them, including the potentially high cost of conducting long-term studies and the possible introduction of selective attrition over time. However, one likely factor on which we focus here is the relative lack of attention that has been paid to these rather complex issues in both the substantive and quantitative disciplines of psychology. In intensive longitudinal suicide research, interpersonal factors are typically distinguished as within-person and between-person constructs, with each level capturing different sources of variation. Within-person interpersonal factors refer to moment-to-moment or day-to-day interpersonal experiences that vary across occasions within the same individual. Examples in the evidence include interpersonal negative life events (NLEs), thwarted belongingness, perceived burdensomeness, and relationship dynamics such as conflict, support, attachment, and emotion regulation. The N1 evidence explicitly identifies interpersonal NLEs, including loss, difficulties or conflict with family, friends, and romantic partners, and notes that such events are common in the month prior to a suicide attempt in adults [N1-R1]. The N1-F1 evidence further supports this by describing daily assessments of interpersonal NLEs and fluctuations in thwarted belongingness with family and friends, as well as suicidal thoughts, using an intensive longitudinal design [N1-F1]. Similarly, the N4-F4 evidence states that research increasingly links suicidal thoughts and behaviors to interpersonal phenomenon such as appraisals of burdensomeness, experienced loneliness, and thwarted belongingness [N4-F4].

Between-person interpersonal factors refer to stable or relatively stable characteristics of the social context across individuals. Examples in the evidence include relationship quality, family structure, and social network composition. The N1-F1 evidence notes that interpersonal NLEs are related to family and peer relationships, with specific mention of family conflict, rejection, peers rejection, exclusion, victimization, and romantic partner break-ups as most strongly linked to STBs among adolescents [N1-F1]. The N1-R1 evidence also emphasizes that interpersonal NLEs are robustly related to suicide risk across the lifespan [N1-R1]. In addition, the N4-F4 evidence explicitly discusses dyadic methodological considerations and notes that interpersonal phenomenon are often assessed through individuals’ perceptions of burdensomeness, loneliness, and belongingness, which suggests that between-person constructs are operationalized through stable or relatively stable contextual features of relationships rather than momentary interpersonal states [N4-F4].

Operationally, these factors are measured in longitudinal studies using repeated assessments over time. Within-person factors are captured through frequent repeated measures and ecological momentary assessment (EMA) or daily diary methods, which allow researchers to observe variation within the same person across days or time points. The N1-F1 evidence provides a concrete example of this, using smartphone-based EMA to measure presence of interpersonal NLEs at the day level and fluctuations in thwarted belongingness and suicidal thoughts within day [N1-F1]. The N2-F2 evidence similarly describes intensive longitudinal methods as involving repeatedly assessing individuals over short periods of time, with EMA and daily diary as common methodologies [N2-F2]. For between-person factors, the evidence suggests that researchers assess stable contextual features such as family structure, relationship quality, and social network composition, even though the provided citations do not give detailed operational definitions for every construct. The N4-F4 evidence indicates that dyadic methodological approaches consider partner-level and couple-level effects, and that interpersonal phenomenon can be operationalized through appraisals and relationship dynamics [N4-F4]. The N4-R1 evidence also points to dyadic associations of suicidal risk predicting relational satisfaction in couples, which implies that between-person constructs are measured through relational outcomes and couple-level variables [N4-R1].

Taken together, the evidence supports a clear distinction: within-person interpersonal factors are experienced and measured as momentary or state-like interpersonal experiences, while between-person interpersonal factors are more contextual and stable features of the social environment. The methodological framing provided by the intensive longitudinal studies emphasizes repeated assessment for within-person variation, whereas between-person variation is inferred from stable relationship features and dyadic constructs [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

Intensive longitudinal design supports the study of interpersonal factors in suicidal behaviors by capturing within-person variation through frequent repeated measures and ecological momentary assessment. The N2-F2 evidence states that intensive longitudinal methods, such as ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and daily diary, involve repeatedly assessing individuals over short periods of time, which is important for studying suicidal thoughts and behaviors because these outcomes vary over short periods [N2-F2]. The same source also emphasizes that ILM are feasible and do not have a negative impact on participants, while the N2-R1 evidence notes that ILM involve repeatedly assessing individuals and are increasingly used to study STBs [N2-R1]. The N2-R5 excerpt adds that EMA is increasingly used to study suicidal thoughts and behaviors and highlights ethical considerations, which shows that the design is being actively applied to dynamic suicidal behaviors [N2-R5]. The N1-F1 evidence provides a direct example of this support, using smartphone-based EMA to capture day-level interpersonal NLEs and within-day fluctuations in thwarted belongingness and suicidal thoughts [N1-F1].

At the same time, intensive longitudinal design has important constraints. One major constraint is that panel and cross-sectional designs differ in how well they separate within-person and between-person effects. The N5-F3 evidence explicitly discusses longitudinal models and notes that traditional cross-sectional assessments are poorly suited for evaluating within-person processes, whereas longitudinal designs allow for the separation of between-person and within-person effects [N5-F3]. It also explains that the ability to disaggregate these effects has not been fully capitalized upon in many social science applications, indicating that researchers must be careful not to misinterpret effects from cross-sectional data as within-person effects [N5-F3]. The N5-F3 source further notes that longitudinal data are increasingly used because they allow for the proper separation of these effects, but that this opportunity is not always fully realized [N5-F3].

Methodological limitations of intensive longitudinal studies include attrition, sampling, and measurement error. The N5-F3 evidence explicitly mentions that one likely factor limiting full use of longitudinal data is the relative lack of attention to these complex issues, as well as the high cost of long-term studies and possible selective attrition [N5-F3]. It also notes that researchers may not fully capitalize on the opportunity because of analytic challenges and because the substantive literature has not always emphasized the importance of disaggregating effects [N5-F3]. The N2-F2 evidence similarly notes that few studies have used ILM to study suicidality in diverse samples, which points to sampling limitations [N2-F2]. The N2-R3 evidence adds that engagement with EMA can be difficult to measure and that participant engagement is a topic of active research, which implies that measurement error and response bias may be relevant [N2-R3].

Overall, intensive longitudinal design is highly supportive of studying within-person interpersonal factors because it allows frequent capture of momentary variation through EMA and daily diary. However, it is constrained by the need to carefully distinguish longitudinal from cross-sectional designs and by the limitations of attrition, sampling, and measurement error [N2-F2][N5-F3][N2-R3].

Studying interpersonal factors and suicidal behaviors in intensive longitudinal research raises several causal and interpretive issues, especially regarding direction of causality, confounding by stable individual traits, and interpretation of moderation and mediation across levels and time.

Direction of causality and reverse causation concerns are central. The N1-F1 evidence shows that interpersonal NLEs predict next-day suicidal thoughts, but it also implies that other pathways may be present and that the relationship is not necessarily bidirectional in a single direction [N1-F1]. The N3-R1 evidence similarly states that most studies provide evidence of a strong direct relationship between perceived burden and suicidal ideation, which suggests that the observed associations may reflect causal effects, but does not by itself rule out reverse causation or confounding [N3-R1]. The N5-F3 evidence emphasizes that longitudinal data are important because they allow for the separation of between-person and within-person effects, which is critical when evaluating theories that posit effects at one level of analysis but are tested at another [N5-F3]. This means that researchers must be cautious about interpreting observed associations as causal without carefully considering whether the direction of influence is from the interpersonal factor to suicidal behavior or vice versa.

Confounding by stable individual traits versus changing contextual factors is another major issue. The N6-R1 evidence notes that psychosocial crises and psychiatric disorders may constitute the stress component of stress-diathesis models of suicidal behavior [N6-R1]. This aligns with the broader evidence base that individual-level traits and contextual stressors may both contribute to suicidal behavior. The N5-F3 evidence explicitly distinguishes between within-person processes and between-person processes, noting that theories often posit within-person effects, yet standard cross-sectional designs test effects at a different level [N5-F3]. This distinction is important because stable individual differences can confound within-person associations if they are not controlled. The N6-R4 evidence also points to psychosocial stressors such as perceived discrimination and acculturation as factors affecting well-being, which underscores the importance of distinguishing stable individual characteristics from changing contextual stressors [N6-R4]. The N1-F1 evidence further illustrates this by showing that interpersonal NLEs are linked to suicidal thoughts, but that the relationship is mediated by thwarted belongingness, which suggests that stable contextual features and changing contextual features may both matter [N1-F1].

Interpretation of moderation and mediation across levels and time is complicated. The N3-R3 evidence describes a moderated mediation model used to explore the longitudinal relationship between cyberbullying perpetration and suicidal behavior, indicating that moderation and mediation are common analytic strategies in this literature [N3-R3]. The N3-R5 evidence similarly notes that personality traits can moderate the link between interpersonal dysfunction and suicidal behavior, showing that moderation can occur at the individual level [N3-R5]. The N5-F3 evidence emphasizes that longitudinal models can disaggregate effects over time and that the ability to separate between-person and within-person effects is critical for evaluating theories [N5-F3]. This means that moderation and mediation should be interpreted carefully: a moderator may vary at the individual level, the relationship level, or the contextual level, while mediation may occur within a person across occasions or across persons depending on the model specification [N3-R3][N3-R5][N5-F3]. The N1-F1 evidence provides a concrete example of mediation by showing that family thwarted belongingness and friend thwarted belongingness mediated the association between interpersonal NLEs and next-day suicidal thoughts, although family mediation was stronger than friend mediation [N1-F1]. This illustrates that mediation can be level-specific and time-specific in longitudinal studies.

In sum, the causal and interpretive challenges include reverse causation concerns, confounding by stable individual traits, and the need for careful interpretation of moderation and mediation across levels and time [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5][N5-F3][N6-R1]. Intensive longitudinal design helps mitigate some of these issues by allowing within-person and between-person effects to be separated, but it does not eliminate them entirely [N5-F3].

Dyadic and network-level interpersonal factors differ from dyadic-level interaction effects in both conceptual scope and analytic approach. Dyadic-level interaction effects refer to partner-specific and couple-specific relationships, whereas network-level factors capture broader social ties and peer influence beyond the immediate dyad. The N4-F4 evidence explicitly discusses dyadic methodological considerations and notes that interpersonal phenomenon can be assessed through partner-level and couple-level effects [N4-F4]. The N4-R1 evidence also points to dyadic associations of suicidal risk predicting relational satisfaction in couples, indicating that dyadic analysis often focuses on the relationship between two individuals and their mutual influence [N4-R1]. The N4-R3 evidence supports this broader perspective by stating that suicidal thoughts and behaviors are linked to a range of interpersonal phenomenon, adding support for the value of dyadic inquiry [N4-R3]. The N7-R2 evidence adds that an online daily diary study examined romantic relationship dynamics and mental health indicators in adults over 10 days, further illustrating how dyadic analysis can capture relational processes [N7-R2].

Network-level interpersonal factors, by contrast, extend beyond the dyad to include broader social ties and peer influence. The N4-F4 evidence describes suicide as an interpersonal phenomenon and emphasizes the value of incorporating conceptual models from relationship science, suggesting that network-level factors can be part of a more comprehensive interpersonal framework [N4-F4]. The N4-R4 evidence explicitly discusses dyadic relationships and romantic relationship dynamics, but the N4-F4 evidence also implies that network-level factors are relevant for suicide research because they involve broader social contexts [N4-F4][N4-R4]. The N7-R3 evidence also indicates that dyadic associations of suicidal risk can be understood in terms of relationship dynamics and that addressing risk and protective factors requires partner-level perspectives, which supports the distinction between dyadic and broader network-level factors [N7-R3]. In addition, the N4-F4 evidence mentions that interpersonal phenomenon are often assessed through appraisals of burdensomeness, experienced loneliness, and thwarted belongingness, which can be interpreted as both dyadic and network-level constructs depending on the context [N4-F4].

Analytic approaches used to distinguish dyadic from network-level effects include dyadic models, multilevel models, and actor-partner interdependence models (APIMs). The N4-F4 evidence specifically references actor partner interdependence models and multilevel models as relevant analytic approaches for testing hypotheses derived from conceptual approaches to interpersonal phenomenon [N4-F4]. The N5-F3 evidence also emphasizes multilevel modeling as a way to separate between-person and within-person effects in longitudinal models of change [N5-F3]. In dyadic research, APIMs are particularly useful because they allow researchers to test whether a relationship feature affects one partner, the other partner, or both partners simultaneously [N4-F4]. The N4-F4 evidence further states that it would be valuable to consider conceptual models from relationship science and corresponding methodological approaches, which suggests that analytic strategies should be chosen to match the theoretical level of analysis being tested [N4-F4]. The N5-F3 evidence also notes that mixed-effects models can include multiple random effects per individual and are useful for examining hypotheses about between-person differences in the mean structure, which supports the idea that longitudinal dyadic and network analyses rely on hierarchical modeling [N5-F3].

In practice, dyadic analysis captures partner-level and couple-level effects by modeling mutual influences between two people, while network analysis captures broader social ties and peer influence by including additional nodes and edges in the social structure. The evidence provided does not offer a fully detailed network analysis example, but it does support the distinction through the emphasis on dyadic methodological and statistical considerations, as well as the use of multilevel and APIM approaches [N4-F4][N5-F3]. The N4-R1 and N4-R3 evidence together suggest that dyadic analysis can be used to examine relational satisfaction, suicidal risk, and broader interpersonal phenomenon, whereas network-level analysis would explicitly model the influence of a person’s wider social network [N4-R1][N4-R3]. Overall, the evidence indicates that dyadic-level interaction effects are partner-specific and couple-specific, whereas network-level effects extend to broader social ties and peer influence, and that analytic approaches such as APIMs and multilevel models are used to distinguish these levels [N4-F4][N5-F3].

## Integrated synthesis of how within-person and between-person interpersonal factors differentially relate to suicidal behaviors in intensive longitudinal studies

### 1) Core distinction: within-person versus between-person interpersonal factors

In intensive longitudinal suicide research, interpersonal factors are typically divided into two levels: **within-person** and **between-person** constructs. Within-person factors are momentary or state-like interpersonal experiences that vary across occasions within the same individual. Examples include interpersonal negative life events (NLEs), thwarted belongingness, perceived burdensomeness, loneliness, and relationship dynamics such as conflict, support, attachment, and emotion regulation [N1-R1][N1-F1][N4-F4]. These are measured through repeated assessments and ecological momentary assessment (EMA) or daily diary methods, which allow researchers to capture fluctuating interpersonal experiences over time [N2-F2][N1-F1].

Between-person interpersonal factors, by contrast, refer to stable or relatively stable characteristics of the social context across individuals. Examples in the evidence include relationship quality, family structure, and social network composition [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The evidence also points to dyadic associations of suicidal risk predicting relational satisfaction in couples, indicating that between-person constructs are often operationalized through relational outcomes and couple-level variables [N4-R1]. In other words, between-person constructs are broader contextual features that may remain relatively stable across occasions, whereas within-person constructs are more momentary and variable within a single person [N1-F1][N4-F4].

### 2) How intensive longitudinal design supports and constrains these distinctions

Intensive longitudinal design is especially supportive of studying within-person interpersonal factors because it allows researchers to capture **within-person variation** through frequent repeated measures and EMA/daily diary methods. The evidence shows that intensive longitudinal methods involve repeatedly assessing individuals over short periods of time, which is important for studying outcomes that vary over short periods such as suicidal thoughts and behaviors [N2-F2]. The N1-F1 evidence provides a concrete example of this: smartphone-based EMA was used to measure day-level interpersonal NLEs and within-day fluctuations in thwarted belongingness and suicidal thoughts [N1-F1].

At the same time, intensive longitudinal design has important constraints. One major constraint is the need to distinguish **panel and cross-sectional designs** in how they separate within-person and between-person effects. The branch report notes that traditional cross-sectional assessments are poorly suited for evaluating within-person processes, whereas longitudinal designs allow for the separation of between-person and within-person effects [N5-F3]. The evidence also emphasizes that longitudinal data are increasingly used because they allow for the proper separation of these effects, but that this opportunity is not always fully realized [N5-F3]. That means researchers must be careful not to misinterpret effects from cross-sectional data as within-person effects.

Other limitations include **attrition, sampling, and measurement error**. The branch report states that intensive longitudinal studies may be constrained by attrition, sampling limitations, and measurement issues [N5-F3][N2-R3]. The evidence also notes that few studies have used ILM to study suicidality in diverse samples, which points to sampling constraints [N2-F2]. The N2-R3 evidence further highlights engagement with EMA as a topic of active research, implying that measurement error and response bias may affect results [N2-R3].

### 3) Differential relationships to suicidal behaviors

The evidence suggests that within-person and between-person interpersonal factors differentially relate to suicidal behaviors in at least three ways.

First, **within-person interpersonal factors often operate as immediate or short-term triggers**. The N1-F1 evidence shows that interpersonal NLEs predicted next-day suicidal thoughts in high-risk adolescents, and that family thwarted belongingness and friend thwarted belongingness mediated the association between interpersonal NLEs and suicidal thoughts [N1-F1]. This suggests that momentary interpersonal stressors can amplify suicidal thoughts on a subsequent day. The evidence also notes that depressive symptoms were related to greater negative affect and lower positive affect, meaning that within-person mood states can shape interpersonal experiences and suicidal risk [N1-F1].

Second, **between-person interpersonal factors often operate as more stable contextual influences**. The N1-F1 evidence indicates that interpersonal NLEs are linked to family and peer relationships, with specific interpersonal events such as conflict, rejection, exclusion, victimization, and romantic partner break-ups being strongly associated with STBs among adolescents [N1-F1]. The N4-F4 evidence adds that dyadic methodological considerations are important because interpersonal phenomenon can be assessed through partner-level and couple-level effects [N4-F4]. This implies that stable relationship features and broader social context matter for suicide risk.

Third, **both levels can interact in complex ways**. The evidence includes examples of mediation and moderation across levels and time. ### 1) Core distinction: within-person versus between-person interpersonal factors

In intensive longitudinal suicide research, interpersonal factors are typically divided into two levels: **within-person** and **between-person** constructs. Within-person factors are momentary or state-like interpersonal experiences that vary across occasions within the same individual. These are measured through repeated assessments and ecological momentary assessment (EMA) or daily diary methods, which allow researchers to capture fluctuating interpersonal experiences over time [N2-F2][N1-F1].

Between-person interpersonal factors, by contrast, refer to stable or relatively stable characteristics of the social context across individuals. Examples in the evidence include relationship quality, family structure, and social network composition [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The evidence also points to dyadic associations of suicidal risk predicting relational satisfaction in couples, indicating that between-person constructs are often operationalized through relational outcomes and couple-level variables [N4-R1]. In other words, between-person constructs are broader contextual features that may remain relatively stable across occasions, whereas within-person constructs are more momentary and variable within a single person [N1-F1][N4-F4].

### 2) How intensive longitudinal design supports and constrains these distinctions

Intensive longitudinal design is especially supportive of studying within-person interpersonal factors because it allows researchers to capture **within-person variation** through frequent repeated measures and EMA/daily diary methods. The evidence shows that intensive longitudinal methods involve repeatedly assessing individuals over short periods of time, which is important for studying outcomes that vary over short periods such as suicidal thoughts and behaviors [N2-F2]. The N1-F1 evidence provides a concrete example of this: smartphone-based EMA was used to measure day-level interpersonal NLEs and within-day fluctuations in thwarted belongingness and suicidal thoughts [N1-F1].

At the same time, intensive longitudinal design has important constraints. One major constraint is the need to distinguish **panel and cross-sectional designs** in how they separate within-person and between-person effects. The branch report notes that traditional cross-sectional assessments are poorly suited for evaluating within-person processes, whereas longitudinal designs allow for the separation of between-person and within-person effects [N5-F3]. The evidence also emphasizes that longitudinal data are increasingly used because they allow for the proper separation of these effects, but that this opportunity is not always fully realized [N5-F3]. That means researchers must be careful not to misinterpret effects from cross-sectional data as within-person effects.

Other limitations include **attrition, sampling, and measurement error**. The branch report states that intensive longitudinal studies may be constrained by attrition, sampling limitations, and measurement issues [N5-F3][N2-R3]. The evidence also notes that few studies have used ILM to study suicidality in diverse samples, which points to sampling constraints [N2-F2]. The N2-R3 evidence further highlights engagement with EMA as a topic of active research, implying that measurement error and response bias may affect results [N2-R3].

### 3) Differential relationships to suicidal behaviors

The evidence suggests that within-person and between-person interpersonal factors differentially relate to suicidal behaviors in at least three ways.

First, **within-person interpersonal factors often operate as immediate or short-term triggers**. The N1-F1 evidence shows that interpersonal NLEs predicted next-day suicidal thoughts in high-risk adolescents, and that family thwarted belongingness and friend thwarted belongingness mediated the association between interpersonal NLEs and suicidal thoughts [N1-F1]. This suggests that momentary interpersonal stressors can amplify suicidal thoughts on a subsequent day. The evidence also notes that depressive symptoms were related to greater negative affect and lower positive affect, meaning that within-person mood states can shape interpersonal experiences and suicidal risk [N1-F1].

Second, **between-person interpersonal factors often operate as more stable contextual influences**. The N1-F1 evidence indicates that interpersonal NLEs are linked to family and peer relationships, with specific interpersonal events such as conflict, rejection, exclusion, victimization, and romantic partner break-ups being strongly associated with STBs among adolescents [N1-F1]. The N4-F4 evidence adds that dyadic methodological considerations are important because interpersonal phenomenon can be assessed through partner-level and couple-level effects [N4-F4]. This implies that stable relationship features and broader social context matter for suicide risk.

Third, **both levels can interact in complex ways**. The evidence includes examples of mediation and moderation across levels and time. The N3-R3 evidence describes a moderated mediation model used to explore the longitudinal relationship between cyberbullying perpetration and suicidal behavior [N3-R3]. The N3-R5 evidence similarly notes that personality traits can moderate the link between interpersonal dysfunction and suicidal behavior [N3-R5]. The branch report also emphasizes that longitudinal models can disaggregate effects over time and that separation of between-person and within-person effects is critical for evaluating theories [N5-F3]. This means that suicidal behaviors may be shaped by a combination of momentary interpersonal stressors, stable contextual features, and individual-level moderators.

Studying these relationships raises important causal and interpretive issues. One major issue is **direction of causality and reverse causation**. The N3-R1 evidence notes that most studies provide evidence of a strong direct relationship between perceived burden and suicidal ideation, which suggests that associations may reflect causal effects, but does not by itself rule out reverse causation or confounding [N3-R1].
